sm: This is a bonus interview on Grammar Girl with linguist Colin Gorrie, who runs the Dead Language Society newsletter and teaches Old English, Latin and Old Norse online. The question is whether Americans speak more like Shakespeare than British people do. Gorrie says news stories often claim some remote village speaks the closest English to Shakespeare, but no single modern dialect really does, because English has changed everywhere in different ways. He explains that Shakespeare would have pronounced the R in words like car, as most American accents do, and that most American dialects also keep the older short A in path rather than the broad A that arose in England.

Gorrie explains that some early American accents also had the broad A, and that non-rhotic accents like Boston's probably came from transatlantic trade with England. He notes that Noah Webster preferred the path pronunciation, ironically the one Americans did not adopt. Gorrie, who is Canadian, says the Canadian vowel in about may be a survival of an older sound closer to Shakespeare's. He adds that turning T into a D sound in words like better and metal is purely a North American innovation. The host and Gorrie then discuss glottalization of T, which is common in England, as in bottle, and in North American words like kitten.

Gorrie and the host note that Americans drop some prepositions that Britons keep, such as saying wonder the same thing instead of wonder about it. Gorrie concludes that nobody speaks more like Shakespeare. Every dialect has kept some old features and lost others, and piecing them together teaches us about the past. He describes his paid book club, which read Beowulf last year and is now reading Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, sometimes in reconstructed pronunciation. For his first book recommendation he names Proto by Laura Spinney, about the deep past of the Indo-European languages, combining linguistics, archaeology and ancient DNA.

The host says she is listening to Proto as an audiobook and keeps falling asleep to the soothing narrator. Gorrie's second recommendation is Why Q Needs U by Danny Bate, a book on the alphabet and the hidden logic of English spelling. His third is The Worm Ouroboros, an early twentieth century fantasy novel by E. R. Eddison, written in faithful seventeenth century English, with some passages in even older forms. He says Tolkien liked it, and C. S. Lewis said he would take it to a desert island. Gorrie says his home base is his Dead Language Society newsletter on Substack, and the host thanks him for the interview.
